hook: An RTX 4090 runs over a hundred thousand threads at once. Every kernel trick in this module comes from how those threads share memory.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — An RTX 4090 runs over a hundred thousand threads at once. Every kernel trick in this module comes from how those threads share memory.

0:15 QUESTION — FlashAttention, the speedrun's FP8 kernels and every inference engine exist because of a few hardware facts: thousands of small cores grouped into SMs, warps of 32 that move in lockstep, and a memory hierarchy where the fast memory is tiny. What does the GPU we are renting actually look like?

1:00 INTUITION — A GPU is a factory of 128 workshops called SMs. Each workshop runs squads of 32 workers called warps that all execute the same instruction. There is one huge slow warehouse, HBM or here GDDR6X, a shared loading dock called L2, and inside each workshop a small fast shelf called shared memory plus each worker's own pockets, the registers. [EXPLAINER plays here]

3:00 MATH — Peak numbers from the spec sheet, derived not memorized. FP32 compute: 128 SMs x 128 FP32 lanes x 2 FLOPs per FMA x 2.52 GHz boost = 82.6 TFLOPS. Memory bandwidth: 384-bit bus x 21 Gbps per pin / 8 = 1008 GB/s. Ratio: 82.6e12 / 1.008e12 = 82 FLOPs per byte, so a kernel must do about 82 FLOPs per byte loaded or it waits on memory. Occupancy limits per SM on compute capability 8.9: 1536 threads (48 warps), 64K 32-bit registers, up to 100 KB shared memory. So a kernel using 128 registers per thread fits at most 65536/128 = 512 threads per SM.

6:00 CODE — On a RunPod RTX 4090 pod (PyTorch template). nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,memory.total,clocks.max.sm,clocks.max.memory,power.limit --format=csv. In Python: p = torch.cuda.get_device_properties(0); print(p) and p.multi_processor_count, p.total_memory, p.major, p.minor. Then a 20-line device_query.cu: cudaGetDeviceProperties(&prop, 0) and print prop.multiProcessorCount, prop.sharedMemPerMultiprocessor, prop.sharedMemPerBlockOptin, prop.regsPerMultiprocessor, prop.maxThreadsPerMultiProcessor, prop.l2CacheSize, prop.memoryBusWidth, prop.warpSize. nvcc -O3 -arch=sm_89 device_query.cu -o dq && ./dq. Build the annotated diagram from these numbers.

9:00 RECEIPT — Assert against NVIDIA's published Ada specs: multiProcessorCount == 128, warpSize == 32, major.minor == 8.9, memoryBusWidth == 384, l2CacheSize == 75497472 bytes (72 MB), total memory about 24 GB. Then compute peak FP32 from the measured max SM clock instead of the spec boost clock, and note your card may boost above 2.52 GHz.
10:30 MEASURE — The annotated diagram with every number filled in from your own pod, plus one derived number on screen: the 82 FLOPs per byte ridge point, which is the subject of the next episode.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Compute is cheap and memory traffic is expensive, by almost two orders of magnitude. Interview line: 'On a 4090 you need about 80 FLOPs per byte of DRAM traffic to be compute-bound, so most elementwise and normalization kernels are memory-bound.' This module builds toward P1, feather-attn.
12:00 NEXT — Next: Roofline and arithmetic intensity
key_math: peak_FP32 = n_SM x lanes_per_SM x 2 x f_clock = 128 x 128 x 2 x 2.52e9 = 82.6 TFLOPS; BW = 384 bit x 21 Gbps / 8 = 1008 GB/s; ridge = 82.6e12/1.008e12 ~= 82 FLOP/byte

gotchas: nvcc without -arch=sm_89 may build for an older target and still run, hiding features; RunPod containers can show a power-limited or clock-locked card, read nvidia-smi before trusting peak numbers; Confusing CUDA cores (marketing count, 16384) with SMs (128) when computing occupancy
interview_q: What is a warp and why does it matter for performance? Model answer: A warp is 32 threads that execute the same instruction together on an SM. Branches that split a warp serialize both paths, and memory accesses from a warp are coalesced into as few transactions as possible, so kernel design is mostly about keeping warps uniform and their accesses contiguous.
explainer: We zoom out on the RTX 4090 die and see one hundred twenty eight identical tiles. Each tile is a streaming multiprocessor.
Inside one SM we see four partitions, and in each, groups of thirty two lanes moving in lockstep. That group is a warp.
Each thread has its own registers, the fastest storage on the chip, sitting right next to the arithmetic units.
The SM also has a small shared memory, up to one hundred kilobytes, that every thread in a block can read and write.
Outside the SMs sits a seventy two megabyte L2 cache, shared by the whole chip.
Far away is twenty four gigabytes of GDDR6X, the main memory. It is huge, but every trip there is slow.
We line up the numbers. Eighty two teraflops of compute, about one terabyte per second of memory. Compute wins by eighty two times.

hook: Vector add on a 4090 uses under one percent of its compute. A big matmul uses most of it. One number tells them apart.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Vector add on a 4090 uses under one percent of its compute. A big matmul uses most of it. One number tells them apart.

0:15 QUESTION — Horace He's 'Go Brrrr' and DeepMind's scaling book both start here: before optimizing a kernel, decide whether it is limited by compute or by memory. Getting this wrong is how people spend a week speeding up the wrong thing.

1:00 INTUITION — Arithmetic intensity is FLOPs divided by bytes moved to and from main memory. The roofline is a ceiling with a slanted part, where bandwidth limits you, and a flat part, where compute limits you. Each kernel is a dot below that roof. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Roofline: attainable FLOP/s = min(peak_FLOPs, I x BW). Ridge I* = peak/BW = 82 FLOP/byte for FP32 CUDA cores on the 4090 (about 164 for BF16 tensor cores at 165 TFLOPS). Elementwise add in fp32: 1 FLOP per element, 12 bytes (two reads, one write), I = 0.083. GELU is maybe 10 to 20 FLOPs per 8 bytes, still far below the ridge. Square matmul N x N x N in fp32 with perfect reuse: 2N^3 FLOPs over 3 x 4 x N^2 bytes, I = N/6; crosses the ridge at N ~ 490. Softmax over a row: a handful of FLOPs per element, 8 bytes: memory-bound.

5:30 CODE — Helper (preview of M07E18): def time_ms(fn, warmup=10, iters=100) using torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True), record, torch.cuda.synchronize(), elapsed_time / iters. Ops: a + b for n = 2^28; torch.nn.functional.gelu; torch.softmax over (8192, 8192); torch.matmul for N in [128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192] in fp32 with torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = False. For each, compute FLOPs and minimal bytes analytically, then achieved FLOP/s and GB/s. Plot on log-log axes with the two roofs.

9:00 RECEIPT — Memory-bound ops: achieved GB/s for a + b should be 85 to 95 percent of 1008 GB/s, and no op may plot above the roof (if one does, your byte count is wrong or L2 is caching it). Compute-bound: fp32 matmul at N = 8192 should land at a large fraction of 82.6 TFLOPS; print the percent. Published check: the slope-to-flat transition sits near I = 82, the ridge we derived in M07E01.
11:00 MEASURE — The roofline plot with every op as a labeled dot, plus a table: op, intensity, achieved, percent of roof. The matmul dots walk up the slanted line and flatten as N grows.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Compute intensity first, then optimize: memory-bound kernels need fewer bytes, compute-bound kernels need better use of the ALUs. Interview line: 'Arithmetic intensity versus the ridge point tells me whether to fuse and cut traffic or to tile and feed tensor cores.'
12:30 NEXT — Next: Profiling PyTorch
key_math: perf = min(P_peak, I x BW); I = FLOPs / bytes; add fp32: I = 1/12; square matmul: I = 2N^3 / (12 N^2) = N/6; ridge I* = 82 (FP32), ~164 (BF16 tensor)
code_task: time_ms(fn) with CUDA events after warmup; roofline.py measuring add, gelu, softmax and fp32 matmul over N, computing intensity and achieved FLOP/s, plotting against the 4090 roofs.
receipt: a + b reaches ~85-95% of 1008 GB/s; no point exceeds the roof; fp32 matmul at N=8192 reported as % of 82.6 TFLOPS; transition near the derived ridge I* ~= 82.
gotchas: Measuring arrays smaller than the 72 MB L2 makes memory-bound ops look faster than DRAM allows; Forgetting allow_tf32=False puts fp32 matmul on tensor cores under a different roof; Counting bytes from intermediate tensors that a kernel never actually writes
interview_q: Is LayerNorm compute-bound or memory-bound on a modern GPU? Model answer: Memory-bound. It does a few FLOPs per element but must read and write every element, giving an arithmetic intensity of order 1 FLOP per byte, far below a ridge of 80 to 300. The fix is fusion to cut memory traffic, not faster math.
explainer: We draw log log axes. Horizontal is arithmetic intensity, FLOPs per byte. Vertical is achieved FLOPs per second.
A slanted line rises from the left. Its height is bandwidth times intensity, the memory roof.
A flat line runs across the top at eighty two teraflops. That is the compute roof.
They meet at the ridge, eighty two FLOPs per byte. Left of it, memory limits you. Right of it, compute does.
We drop in vector add at one twelfth of a FLOP per byte. It sits on the slanted line, far left, starved for data.
Now matmul dots for growing sizes walk up the slope, cross the ridge, and flatten under the compute roof.
So the first question for any kernel is where its dot lives. That decides what kind of optimization can help.

hook: I assumed attention was the slow part of my GPT. The profiler said otherwise. Here is how to read a trace in ten minutes.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — I assumed attention was the slow part of my GPT. The profiler said otherwise. Here is how to read a trace in ten minutes.

0:15 QUESTION — Every performance team at a lab starts with a trace, not a guess. PyTorch ships torch.profiler and the trace opens in Perfetto. Where does the time in one GPT training step actually go?

1:00 INTUITION — The trace is two timelines stacked: the CPU thread queuing up work and the GPU stream doing it. If the GPU row has gaps, you are launch-bound or waiting on the CPU. If it is solid, the widest blocks are your bottleneck. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Expected split from FLOP counting (M05E16): matmul FLOPs per step ~ 6 N tokens; attention score FLOPs ~ 12 L T d per token, small at T = 256 relative to the 24 L d^2 of the weights. So at short context the GEMMs should dominate time, and elementwise ops should take a share far larger than their FLOP share because they are memory-bound. MFU = achieved model FLOPs / peak: 6 N tokens_per_step / (step_time x peak).

4:30 CODE — Move the M06E09 GPT to the 4090 with bf16 autocast. from torch.profiler import profile, ProfilerActivity, schedule, record_function. with profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.CUDA], schedule=schedule(wait=1, warmup=2, active=3), record_shapes=True, with_stack=False) as prof: for step in range(6): train_step(); prof.step(). Wrap phases with record_function('forward'), ('backward'), ('optimizer'). print(prof.key_averages().table(sort_by='cuda_time_total', row_limit=15)) (newer releases also accept 'device_time_total'). prof.export_chrome_trace('trace.json') and open it in ui.perfetto.dev.

8:00 RECEIPT — Sum of GPU kernel time in the active window should equal the CUDA-event-measured step time minus idle gaps; check they agree within about 10 percent. Name the top three kernels by GPU time: expect cuBLAS GEMM kernels first (names containing gemm), then likely the SDPA attention kernel or the cross-entropy / softmax over the 10k vocab, then an elementwise or optimizer kernel. Compare GEMM share of time to its FLOP share from the formula.

10:00 MEASURE — Pie chart: GEMM, attention, elementwise and norm, optimizer, idle. MFU number for the step. One concrete fix suggested by the trace (for example torch.compile for the elementwise share, or the fused AdamW via torch.optim.AdamW(fused=True)) with before and after step time.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Profile first, then optimize the widest block on the GPU timeline. Interview line: 'I look for GPU idle gaps first, launch overhead or syncs, then the top kernels by device time, then compare time share to FLOP share to find memory-bound waste.'
12:00 NEXT — Next: CUDA 101: vector add
key_math: MFU = 6 N (tokens/step) / (t_step x P_peak); FLOPs/token ~= 6N + 12 L T d (attention scores); time share vs FLOP share reveals memory-bound ops
code_task: profile_step.py: torch.profiler.profile with CPU+CUDA activities and schedule(wait=1, warmup=2, active=3), record_function regions, key_averages table, export_chrome_trace for Perfetto; MFU calculation.
receipt: Total GPU kernel time in the trace agrees with CUDA-event step time (minus idle) within ~10%; top-3 kernels named with their share; measured GEMM share compared to the 6N FLOP prediction.
gotchas: Profiling the first steps captures cuBLAS heuristics and allocator warmup, use the schedule's warmup; Calling .item() for logging inside the step inserts a sync that shows as a GPU gap; Reading CPU time columns as GPU time, sort by the CUDA or device column
interview_q: Your training step is slower than expected. How do you find out why? Model answer: Take a torch.profiler trace over a few steady-state steps and open it in Perfetto. Check for GPU idle gaps (launch overhead, host syncs, data loading), then rank kernels by device time and compare against expected FLOPs to see which are memory-bound or poorly configured.
explainer: We open a trace and see two long horizontal rows. The top row is the CPU thread, the bottom row is the GPU stream.
The CPU row is a flurry of small blocks, each one a kernel launch being queued.
The GPU row has blocks of different widths. Width is time. The widest blocks are where our step goes.
We color the GPU blocks: matmuls in blue, attention in purple, elementwise and norms in orange, optimizer in green.
Blue is the biggest slice, as the FLOP math predicted. But orange is far wider than its tiny share of FLOPs.
Here and there the GPU row has white gaps. Those are moments the GPU sat idle, waiting for the CPU.
So the trace tells us two things to fix: fuse the orange, and close the gaps.

hook: My first CUDA kernel is four lines long, and it moves data at about nine hundred gigabytes per second. Here is every line.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — My first CUDA kernel is four lines long, and it moves data at about nine hundred gigabytes per second. Here is every line.

0:15 QUESTION — PMPP chapter 2 starts with vector addition because it has every concept and none of the difficulty: kernels, threads, blocks, grids, and the index math that every kernel in FlashAttention also uses. How do a million threads each know which element is theirs?

1:00 INTUITION — You write the code for one thread. CUDA launches a grid of blocks, each block a team of threads, and every thread computes its global index from its block number and its position in the block. It is like seat numbers: row times seats per row plus seat. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x. Number of blocks = ceil(n / blockDim) = (n + blockDim - 1) / blockDim. The guard if (i < n) handles the tail. Bytes moved = 3 x 4 x n (read A, read B, write C). Effective bandwidth = 12 n / t. FLOPs = n, so intensity is 1/12: this kernel can only ever be bandwidth-bound, and our target is the 1008 GB/s roof.

4:30 CODE — vector_add.cu: __global__ void vecAdd(const float* A, const float* B, float* C, int n) { int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x; if (i < n) C[i] = A[i] + B[i]; }. Host: cudaMalloc three buffers of n = 1 << 28 floats (1 GB each, well above the 72 MB L2), cudaMemcpy inputs, launch vecAdd<<<(n + 255) / 256, 256>>>(dA, dB, dC, n); check cudaGetLastError(). Time with cudaEventCreate, cudaEventRecord(start), 10 warmup launches first, then 100 timed launches, cudaEventSynchronize(stop), cudaEventElapsedTime. Copy back, compare against a CPU loop. Compile: nvcc -O3 -arch=sm_89 vector_add.cu -o vadd. In Python, time torch.add on the same sizes with torch.cuda.Event after warmup (full bench helper comes in M07E18).

8:30 RECEIPT — Correctness: max |C - (A + B)| == 0 against the CPU result (fp32 add is exact here). Speed: effective GB/s from my kernel vs torch.add(a, b, out=c) on the same buffers vs the 1008 GB/s peak. Expect both around 85 to 92 percent of peak, and mine within a few percent of PyTorch's.

10:00 MEASURE — Bar chart: my kernel, torch.add, theoretical peak. Second chart: GB/s vs block size (32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024) and vs n from 1K to 256M elements, showing small sizes are launch-latency bound and sizes below 72 MB benefit from L2.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — One thread per element, a global index, a bounds guard, and you are at the memory roof. Interview line: 'Vector add has intensity 1/12, so the only metric that matters is effective bandwidth against the DRAM peak.'
12:00 NEXT — Next: The memory hierarchy and coalescing

interview_q: How do you compute a global thread index in a 1D CUDA kernel, and why the bounds check? Model answer: i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x. The grid is rounded up to whole blocks, so the last block has threads past the end of the array that must do nothing.
explainer: We see a long array of one million numbers, A on top, B below, and an empty array C waiting for answers.
We split the arrays into blocks of two hundred fifty six elements each, drawn as colored segments.
Each block becomes a team of two hundred fifty six threads. Every thread grabs one element from A and one from B.
A thread finds its element with one formula: block index times block size, plus its position inside the block.
All the threads add at the same time, and each one writes exactly one result into its slot in C.
The last block hangs off the end of the array. Its extra threads check the bound and do nothing.
The whole thing finishes at about nine hundred gigabytes per second, close to the memory's limit.

hook: Same kernel, same bytes, one index changed. It goes eight times slower. That index decides whether a warp's loads get coalesced.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Same kernel, same bytes, one index changed. It goes eight times slower. That index decides whether a warp's loads get coalesced.

0:15 QUESTION — PMPP chapters 5 and 6 are about the memory hierarchy and the rule that dominates GPU performance: neighboring threads should touch neighboring addresses. FlashAttention's layouts, Simon Boehm's second matmul kernel and every transpose kernel follow from it. Why?

1:00 INTUITION — DRAM does not hand out single floats. It ships 32-byte sectors. When the 32 threads of a warp ask for 32 consecutive floats, that is 128 bytes in four sectors, fully used. When they ask for floats spread far apart, each needs its own sector, and seven eighths of every delivery is thrown away. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — A warp load of 32 fp32 values at stride s (in elements). Bytes requested = 128. Sectors fetched = min(32, ceil(32 s x 4 / 32)) for small s. Stride 1: 4 sectors, 100 percent efficiency. Stride 2: 8 sectors, 50 percent. Stride 8 or more: 32 sectors of 32 bytes each = 1024 bytes for 128 useful, 12.5 percent. So expected effective bandwidth ~ peak x min(1, 1/s) down to peak/8. Shared memory has 32 banks of 4 bytes; a warp reading a column of a 32x32 float tile hits one bank 32 times, a 32-way conflict; padding the row to 33 spreads it across all banks.

5:30 CODE — Kernel 1: strided_copy(const float* in, float* out, int n, int stride): i = global index; out[i] = in[(i * stride) % n] reading at stride, writing coalesced. Sweep stride in 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 on 1 GB arrays. Kernel 2: transpose_naive(in, out, N): out[col * N + row] = in[row * N + col], writes uncoalesced. Kernel 3: transpose_smem with __shared__ float tile[32][32]; load coalesced, __syncthreads(), write coalesced from the transposed tile. Kernel 4: same with tile[32][33] to kill bank conflicts. Time each with cudaEvent after warmup; report effective GB/s = 2 x 4 x elements / t.

9:00 RECEIPT — Correctness: assert transposes equal x.t().contiguous() in PyTorch, called via a tiny load_inline wrapper or by copying back. Speed: stride-1 copy matches torch's x.clone() GB/s within a few percent; the stride sweep follows the predicted peak/s curve flattening at about one eighth; the padded shared-memory transpose reaches a large fraction of copy bandwidth and beats x.t().contiguous() or comes close.
11:00 MEASURE — Plot GB/s vs stride with the theoretical sector-efficiency curve overlaid. Bar chart for the four transpose versions vs clone() bandwidth.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Make consecutive threads touch consecutive addresses in global memory; use shared memory to change the access pattern; pad tiles to avoid bank conflicts. Interview line: 'A naive transpose is slow not from math but from uncoalesced writes; staging through padded shared memory makes both the read and the write coalesced.'
12:30 NEXT — Next: Naive matmul in CUDA
key_math: efficiency(s) = useful bytes / fetched bytes = 128 / (32 B x sectors(s)); s=1: 100%, s=2: 50%, s>=8: 12.5%; bank(addr) = (addr / 4) mod 32; pad tile to [32][33]

receipt: Transposes equal x.t().contiguous(); stride-1 copy within a few % of torch x.clone() bandwidth; measured GB/s vs stride tracks peak x min(1, 1/s) down to ~1/8 peak; padded smem transpose fastest of the four.
gotchas: Arrays that fit in the 72 MB L2 hide the coalescing penalty; Forgetting __syncthreads() between the shared-memory write and read gives racy, mostly-right output; Mixing up row and col with threadIdx.x and threadIdx.y so the 'coalesced' side is the wrong one
interview_q: What is memory coalescing? Model answer: When the threads of a warp access consecutive addresses, the hardware combines them into a few wide memory transactions. Scattered accesses need one transaction per thread and waste most of each fetched sector, cutting effective bandwidth by up to 8x for fp32.
explainer: We see a row of thirty two threads, one warp, and below them a long strip of memory divided into thirty two byte sectors.
In the good case, each thread points at the next float. Their thirty two arrows land in four neighboring sectors.
Four sectors travel up from memory and every single byte gets used. That is what we call a coalesced load.
Now each thread points eight floats apart. The arrows spread across thirty two different sectors.
Thirty two sectors travel up, but only one float in each is used. Seven eighths of the traffic is wasted.
For a transpose, we fix this with shared memory: read rows coalesced into a tile, then write columns from the tile.
One more trap: a tile column lands in a single shared memory bank. Adding one padding column spreads it across all thirty two.

hook: The textbook matmul kernel is twelve lines and runs at about one percent of cuBLAS. Swap two indices and it gets several times faster.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — The textbook matmul kernel is twelve lines and runs at about one percent of cuBLAS. Swap two indices and it gets several times faster.

0:15 QUESTION — Matmul is most of an LLM's FLOPs, and cuBLAS is what PyTorch calls. Simon Boehm's well-known blog climbs from a naive kernel to about 94 percent of cuBLAS on an A6000. This is rung one: PMPP chapter 3's one thread per output element. How bad is it, and why?

1:00 INTUITION — Each thread owns one cell of C and walks along a row of A and a column of B, multiplying and adding. Every thread fetches its own copies from global memory, so the same numbers get loaded thousands of times. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — C = A B with A (M x K), B (K x N). C[r][c] = sum_k A[r][k] B[k][c]. FLOPs = 2 M N K; for M = N = K = 4096 that is 137.4 GFLOP. Naive traffic: each thread loads 2K floats, total 2 M N K x 4 bytes = 550 GB for 4096 cubed if nothing is cached, so intensity is 0.25 FLOP/byte, deep in memory-bound territory. Coalescing: with threadIdx.x mapped to the column c, a warp reads one A value (broadcast) and 32 consecutive B values, coalesced. Mapped to the row r, the warp reads 32 A values K apart, uncoalesced, which is Boehm's kernel 1 vs kernel 2.

5:00 CODE — __global__ void sgemm_naive(int M, int N, int K, const float* A, const float* B, float* C) { int row = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y; int col = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x; if (row < M && col < N) { float acc = 0.f; for (int k = 0; k < K; ++k) acc += A[row*K + k] * B[k*N + col]; C[row*N + col] = acc; } }. dim3 block(32, 32); dim3 grid(ceil(N/32), ceil(M/32)). Second variant with row and col swapped (threadIdx.x on rows) to show the uncoalesced version. Call through load_inline or a standalone nvcc harness; full PyTorch integration is M07E11.

8:00 RECEIPT — Correctness: torch.testing.assert_close(C, A @ B, rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-3) with torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = False so cuBLAS runs true FP32. Speed: GFLOP/s = 2MNK / t for both variants and torch.matmul, at 4096, after warmup with CUDA events. Report percent of cuBLAS and percent of the 82.6 TFLOPS FP32 peak. Published comparison: Boehm's kernel 1 is 1.3 percent of cuBLAS on an A6000 and kernel 2, the coalesced one, 8.5 percent.

11:00 TAKEAWAY — One thread per output is correct and simple, but it reloads the same data thousands of times; the fix is reuse, which is the next episode. Interview line: 'The naive matmul is memory-bound at about 0.25 FLOP/byte; tiling into shared memory raises intensity by the tile width.'

interview_q: Why is a naive CUDA matmul slow even though it has plenty of parallelism? Model answer: Each thread loads a full row and column from global memory, so every element of A and B is loaded N or M times. Intensity is about 0.25 FLOP/byte, far below the ridge, and if threads in a warp map to rows, the loads are uncoalesced as well.
explainer: We see matrices A and B, and an empty output C. One cell of C lights up.
The thread that owns this cell walks across one row of A and down one column of B.
At each step it multiplies a pair and adds to a running sum. After K steps the cell is done.
Now we light up every cell of C at once. Every thread walks its own row and column.
The same row of A is fetched by every thread in that row of C. Thousands of identical trips to memory.
We count the traffic: half a terabyte to compute one hundred thirty seven gigaflops. The arithmetic mostly waits.
Swapping which index runs along the warp makes B's reads coalesced, and the kernel jumps several times faster.

hook: Load a tile once into shared memory, use it thirty-two times. That is the most important idea in GPU programming, and it is fifteen lines.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Load a tile once into shared memory, use it thirty-two times. That is the most important idea in GPU programming, and it is fifteen lines.

0:15 QUESTION — PMPP chapter 5's tiled matmul is the ancestor of every fast kernel: cuBLAS, CUTLASS and FlashAttention all tile. The naive kernel loaded each value thousands of times. How much does sharing it inside a block actually help on a 4090?

1:00 INTUITION — A block of 32 by 32 threads computes a 32 by 32 tile of C. Instead of every thread fetching its own row and column, the block cooperatively copies one 32 by 32 tile of A and one of B into shared memory, everybody uses them, then slides to the next pair of tiles. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — With tile width T, the K dimension is split into K/T phases. In each phase each thread loads one element of A and one of B, then does T multiply-adds from shared memory. Global loads per thread drop from 2K to 2K/T, so intensity rises by a factor of T: 0.25 x 32 = 8 FLOP/byte for T = 32, still below the ridge of 82, which is why this is not the end of the ladder. Shared memory per block: 2 x 32 x 32 x 4 = 8 KB.

5:00 CODE — #define TILE 32. __global__ void sgemm_tiled(int M, int N, int K, const float* A, const float* B, float* C) { __shared__ float As[TILE][TILE]; __shared__ float Bs[TILE][TILE]; int ty = threadIdx.y, tx = threadIdx.x; int row = blockIdx.y*TILE + ty, col = blockIdx.x*TILE + tx; float acc = 0; for (int ph = 0; ph < (K + TILE - 1)/TILE; ++ph) { As[ty][tx] = (row < M && ph*TILE+tx < K) ? A[row*K + ph*TILE + tx] : 0; Bs[ty][tx] = (ph*TILE+ty < K && col < N) ? B[(ph*TILE+ty)*N + col] : 0; __syncthreads(); for (int k = 0; k < TILE; ++k) acc += As[ty][k] * Bs[k][tx]; __syncthreads(); } if (row < M && col < N) C[row*N + col] = acc; }. Explain both __syncthreads(): the first so tiles are fully loaded, the second so nobody overwrites a tile still being read.

8:30 RECEIPT — Correctness: assert_close vs A @ B (allow_tf32 False) at 4096 and at an awkward size like 1000 x 1000 x 1000 to test the bounds. Speed: GFLOP/s vs the coalesced naive kernel from M07E06 and vs cuBLAS. Published comparison: Boehm's shared-memory kernel is 12.8 percent of cuBLAS on an A6000, only about 1.5x his coalesced kernel, because the L1 and L2 caches were already catching a lot of the reuse. Expect a similar modest gain and say so.
10:30 MEASURE — Ladder chart rows so far: naive uncoalesced, naive coalesced, tiled, cuBLAS, in percent of cuBLAS. Plus tile size sweep T = 8, 16, 32.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Tiling raises arithmetic intensity by the tile width, but one output per thread still leaves each thread doing too little work per shared-memory load. Interview line: 'Tiling cuts global traffic by T, but you also need register blocking so each thread computes several outputs per value loaded from shared memory.'

gotchas: Dropping the second __syncthreads() lets fast threads overwrite a tile others are still reading, errors appear only sometimes; Not zero-padding out-of-range tile loads corrupts results when sizes are not multiples of 32; Expecting a 32x speedup from 32x fewer global loads, caches already hid part of the naive kernel's waste
interview_q: Explain tiled matrix multiplication and why it is faster. Model answer: Each block loads a tile of A and a tile of B into shared memory once and all threads reuse them for T multiply-adds before moving to the next tile. This cuts global memory traffic by a factor of the tile width and raises arithmetic intensity accordingly.
explainer: We see the output matrix C divided into a grid of thirty two by thirty two tiles. One tile lights up.
That tile needs a horizontal band of A and a vertical band of B. We chop both bands into square tiles.
The block copies the first A tile and the first B tile into its shared memory, one element per thread.
A barrier called syncthreads holds every thread in the block until both tiles are fully loaded.
Now each thread runs thirty two multiply adds, reading only from the fast shared tiles.
A second barrier, then the block slides to the next pair of tiles and repeats until the band is done.
Each value we fetch from global memory now gets used thirty two times instead of just once.

hook: From two percent of cuBLAS to about ninety, in six kernels. Every rung is one idea, and I measured each one on a 4090.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — From two percent of cuBLAS to about ninety, in six kernels. Every rung is one idea, and I measured each one on a 4090.

0:15 QUESTION — Simon Boehm's 'How to Optimize a CUDA Matmul Kernel for cuBLAS-like Performance' is required reading for kernel interviews at labs. He got from 1.3 percent to 93.7 percent of cuBLAS on an A6000. Do the same rungs pay off on Ada, and which one matters most?

1:00 INTUITION — After tiling, the bottleneck moves from global memory to shared memory and instruction overhead. The fix is to make each thread compute a small block of outputs in registers, so every value read from shared memory is used many times. Then widen the loads and tune the shapes. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Register blocking: a thread computing TM x TN outputs loads TM values of A and TN values of B from shared memory per k step and does TM x TN FMAs. Shared-memory intensity = TM TN / (TM + TN): 1 for 1x1, 8/9 ~ 0.9 for 1D tiling with TM = 8 and TN = 1, 4 for 8x8. Occupancy: blocks per SM = min(1536 / threads_per_block, 65536 / (regs_per_thread x threads), 100 KB / smem_per_block, 24). For BM = BN = 128, BK = 8, 256 threads, smem = (128 + 128) x 8 x 4 = 8 KB, and with about 128 registers per thread the register file allows 2 blocks per SM.

5:30 CODE — Rungs, following Boehm's numbering: kernel 4, 1D blocktiling, each thread computes TM = 8 outputs down a column, BM = BN = 64, BK = 8. Kernel 5, 2D blocktiling, TM = TN = 8, BM = BN = 128, BK = 8, a register array float threadResults[TM*TN], regM[TM], regN[TN] outer product. Kernel 6, vectorized loads: reinterpret_cast<float4*> for 128-bit global loads, store A transposed into shared memory so its reads vectorize too. Kernel 9 style autotuning: a small sweep over BM, BN, BK, TM, TN as template parameters. Kernel 10, warptiling: an extra level so each warp owns a sub-tile, improving register and shared-memory locality. Check resources with nvcc -Xptxas -v (registers and smem per kernel) and cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor.

9:30 RECEIPT — Every rung passes assert_close vs A @ B with allow_tf32 False at 4096. Speed chart in percent of cuBLAS, each next to Boehm's published A6000 number: 1D tiling 36.5, 2D tiling 68.7, vectorized 78.4, autotuned 84.8, warptiling 93.7. Ada has a bigger L2 and different SM balance, so expect the same shape, not the same values. Also report best kernel as percent of the 82.6 TFLOPS FP32 peak.

12:00 MEASURE — The ladder chart, all rungs from M07E06 onward in percent of cuBLAS, with registers per thread and achieved occupancy annotated on each bar. Optional: if Nsight Compute counters are permitted on the pod, ncu --set full on kernels 3 and 5 to show the shared-memory stall reasons shrinking.

13:30 TAKEAWAY — After tiling, the wins come from register blocking: more outputs per thread, more reuse per shared-memory read, then wider loads and tuned shapes. Interview line: 'Each level of the memory hierarchy needs its own tile: block tiles in shared memory, warp tiles, and thread tiles in registers.' The same tiling instincts drive the FlashAttention kernel in P1.
14:00 NEXT — Next: Parallel reduction and warp shuffles

Model answer: Shared-memory bandwidth and instruction overhead, because each thread does one FMA per two shared loads. Register blocking makes each thread compute a TMxTN outer product, so each shared load feeds many FMAs; then vectorize loads, tune tile shapes for occupancy, and add warp-level tiling.
explainer: We draw a ladder with one rung per kernel, and a bar beside each rung showing percent of cuBLAS.
Rung one, naive, barely registers. Rung two, coalesced, and rung three, shared memory tiles, climb a little.
Now one thread computes a column of eight outputs. Each value read from shared memory now feeds eight multiply adds.
Then a thread computes an eight by eight square. An outer product in registers, sixty four results from sixteen loads.
The bar jumps past two thirds of cuBLAS. This is the rung that matters most.
Next, loads widen to four floats at once, and the A tile is stored transposed so those wide loads line up.
Finally, warp tiles add one more level of the hierarchy, and the tuning sweep picks the best shapes.
At each rung, the bottleneck moved one level down the memory hierarchy, closer to the arithmetic units.

hook: Summing a billion numbers sounds trivial. The first GPU version wastes half its threads. Five versions later, it runs at the memory limit.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Summing a billion numbers sounds trivial. The first GPU version wastes half its threads. Five versions later, it runs at the memory limit.

0:15 QUESTION — Reductions are inside softmax, LayerNorm, RMSNorm, loss functions and all-reduce. PMPP chapter 10 builds them step by step. How do thousands of threads add numbers together without fighting, and what is a warp shuffle?

1:00 INTUITION — A reduction is a tournament bracket. Pair up, add, halve, repeat, log n rounds. The trick on a GPU is to keep the winners packed together so whole warps finish at once, and to let the 32 threads of a warp pass values directly through registers instead of through shared memory. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Work: n - 1 additions, depth log2(n). Version 1 (PMPP simple kernel): stride doubles, active threads are 0, 2, 4, ..., so within each warp half the lanes idle: control divergence. Version 2 (convergent): stride halves from blockDim/2, active threads are contiguous 0..stride-1, so whole warps retire. Version 3: shared memory instead of in-place global. Version 4: thread coarsening, each thread first sums C elements serially, fewer blocks and less overhead. Version 5: last 32 values reduced with __shfl_down_sync(0xffffffff, v, offset) for offset 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, then one atomicAdd per block. Target: bytes = 4n, time ~ 4n / 1008 GB/s.

5:30 CODE — reduce_v1_divergent, reduce_v2_convergent, reduce_v3_smem, reduce_v4_coarsened (COARSE_FACTOR template), reduce_v5_shuffle: float v = coarsened partial; for (int off = 16; off > 0; off >>= 1) v += __shfl_down_sync(0xffffffff, v, off); lane 0 of each warp writes to __shared__ float warp_sums[32]; __syncthreads(); first warp reduces warp_sums with shuffles; thread 0 does atomicAdd(out, v). n = 2^28 floats. Time each with CUDA events after warmup.

9:00 RECEIPT — Correctness: compare each result to torch.sum(x.double()).item() with relative error below 1e-5 (fp32 sum order differs, so not exact). Speed: GB/s per version vs torch.sum(x) GB/s vs 1008 GB/s. Expect v5 within a few percent of torch.sum and around 90 percent of peak.
11:00 MEASURE — Bar chart of GB/s for v1 through v5 plus torch.sum, and a small plot of relative error vs n for fp32 tree sum vs a naive serial fp32 sum on the CPU, showing the tree is more accurate.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Keep active threads contiguous, coarsen so each thread does real work, and finish the last 32 with warp shuffles. Interview line: '__shfl_down_sync lets a warp reduce in registers in five steps with no shared memory and no __syncthreads.'

key_math: work = n - 1, depth = log2 n; divergent stride 2^s uses 1/2^s of lanes; shuffle tree: v += shfl_down(v, o) for o in 16,8,4,2,1; t_min = 4n / BW

interview_q: How would you write a fast sum reduction in CUDA? Model answer: Have each thread sum many elements serially with coalesced loads, reduce within a warp using __shfl_down_sync, combine warp results through shared memory, and finish with one atomicAdd or a second pass per block. Keep active threads contiguous to avoid divergence.
explainer: We see sixteen numbers in a row and sixteen threads above them. The goal is one total.
Version one: thread zero adds its neighbor, thread two adds its neighbor, and so on. Every other thread sits idle.
Inside a warp, idle and busy lanes are mixed together, so the warp still pays for every lane.
Version two flips it. The first half of the threads add the second half. Busy threads are packed on the left.
Now whole warps go quiet together as the tree shrinks, and the hardware can simply skip them.
For the last thirty two values, we use a warp shuffle. Lanes pass values to each other directly through registers.
Five shuffle steps, sixteen, eight, four, two, one, and lane zero holds the warp's sum.

hook: Softmax is three loops over a row: max, sum, divide. Doing them in one block, without three trips to memory, is the whole game.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Softmax is three loops over a row: max, sum, divide. Doing them in one block, without three trips to memory, is the whole game.

0:15 QUESTION — Softmax runs on every attention score matrix and on every vocab-sized logit vector. It is memory-bound, so the only question is how many times you read the row. This builds directly toward FlashAttention's online softmax in M08.

1:00 INTUITION — Give each row to one block. The block's threads stride across the row to find the max, combine with the reduction from last episode, then do the same for the sum of exponentials, then write the outputs. If the row fits on chip, keep it there and read DRAM only once. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — y_j = exp(x_j - m) / sum_i exp(x_i - m), m = max_i x_i. Subtracting m changes nothing mathematically (it cancels) and keeps exp from overflowing: exp(89) overflows fp32. Minimum traffic: read M N, write M N, so 8 M N bytes in fp32. A three-pass kernel that rereads x from global memory for the max, the sum and the output reads 3 M N plus writes M N, about 16 M N bytes, half the achievable speed unless the row stays in shared memory or registers or L2 catches the rereads.

5:00 CODE — __global__ void softmax_rows(const float* x, float* y, int M, int N): one block per row, blockDim = 256 or 1024. Pass 1: float m = -INFINITY; for (j = tid; j < N; j += blockDim.x) m = fmaxf(m, row[j]); block_reduce_max(m) using __shfl_down_sync and a shared warp buffer. Pass 2: float s = 0; for (...) s += __expf(row[j] - m); block_reduce_sum(s). Pass 3: for (...) y[j] = __expf(row[j] - m) / s. Version 2: for N up to a few thousand, cache the row in shared memory (extern __shared__ float buf[]) during pass 1 so passes 2 and 3 never touch DRAM. Mention: online softmax computes max and sum in one pass, and that is M08E02.

interview_q: Why subtract the max in softmax, and what makes a softmax kernel fast? Model answer: Subtracting the max cancels mathematically but keeps exp from overflowing. explainer: We see one row of four thousand logits, handed to a single block of two hundred fifty six threads.
The threads stride across the row, each keeping a running max. Then the block reduces those maxes to one number.
Every value has that max subtracted. Now the largest is zero, and exp can never overflow.
The threads stride again, adding up the exponentials, and the block reduces them to one sum.
A third stride writes each exponential divided by the sum. The row now adds to exactly one.
In the naive version, each stride reads the row from main memory again. Three trips.
In the cached version, the row lives in shared memory after the first read. One trip, and the kernel nearly doubles in speed.

hook: A CUDA kernel is useless to a researcher until it is a PyTorch op. load_inline gets you there in one Python file, autograd included.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — A CUDA kernel is useless to a researcher until it is a PyTorch op. load_inline gets you there in one Python file, autograd included.

0:15 QUESTION — Every custom kernel library, from FlashAttention to Liger, ships as PyTorch ops. GPU MODE's first lectures use torch.utils.cpp_extension.load_inline for exactly this. How do you call your matmul from Python and make backward work too?

1:00 INTUITION — Three layers. The CUDA kernel does the math. A small C++ function takes torch::Tensor arguments, checks them, allocates the output and launches the kernel. A torch.autograd.Function on the Python side says how to compute gradients, and for a matmul, the backward is just two more matmuls. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — For C = A B with A (M x K), B (K x N): dL/dA = dL/dC B^T (M x K) and dL/dB = A^T dL/dC (K x N). Check shapes: (M x N)(N x K) = M x K. So backward reuses the same kernel on transposed inputs; .t().contiguous() makes the memory layout match what the kernel expects.

4:30 CODE — cuda_src: the tiled kernel from M07E07 templated on scalar_t, plus torch::Tensor my_matmul(torch::Tensor a, torch::Tensor b) { TORCH_CHECK(a.is_cuda() && b.is_cuda()); TORCH_CHECK(a.size(1) == b.size(0)); a = a.contiguous(); b = b.contiguous(); auto c = torch::empty({a.size(0), b.size(1)}, a.options()); AT_DISPATCH_FLOATING_TYPES(a.scalar_type(), "my_matmul", [&] { kernel<scalar_t><<<grid, block, 0, at::cuda::getCurrentCUDAStream()>>>(...); }); C10_CUDA_KERNEL_LAUNCH_CHECK(); return c; }. cpp_src: 'torch::Tensor my_matmul(torch::Tensor a, torch::Tensor b);'. ext = load_inline(name='my_mm', cpp_sources=cpp_src, cuda_sources=cuda_src, functions=['my_matmul'], extra_cuda_cflags=['-O3'], verbose=True). class MyMatmul(torch.autograd.Function): forward(ctx, a, b): ctx.save_for_backward(a, b); return ext.my_matmul(a, b). backward(ctx, g): a, b = ctx.saved_tensors; return ext.my_matmul(g, b.t()), ext.my_matmul(a.t(), g). Mention the newer path: torch.library.custom_op plus register_autograd and register_fake makes the op work under torch.compile.

hook: Same vector add, same bandwidth as my CUDA version, but written in Python. Triton thinks in blocks, not threads.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Same vector add, same bandwidth as my CUDA version, but written in Python. Triton thinks in blocks, not threads.

0:15 QUESTION — torch.compile generates Triton, the speedrun and Liger use Triton kernels, and OpenAI built Triton so researchers could write fast kernels without CUDA. What is different about the programming model?

1:00 INTUITION — In CUDA you write the code for one thread. In Triton you write the code for one program instance that handles a whole block of elements as a vector. The compiler decides how to map that block onto threads, warps and memory transactions. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Program id pid covers offsets pid*BLOCK + [0, 1, ..., BLOCK-1]. Grid = cdiv(n, BLOCK). The mask offsets < n handles the tail, like the CUDA bounds check but for a vector. Bandwidth math is unchanged: 12 n bytes, I = 1/12, ceiling 1008 GB/s.

4:00 CODE — import triton, triton.language as tl. @triton.jit def add_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, out_ptr, n_elements, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr): pid = tl.program_id(axis=0); offsets = pid * BLOCK_SIZE + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE); mask = offsets < n_elements; x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask); y = tl.load(y_ptr + offsets, mask=mask); tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, x + y, mask=mask). def add(x, y): out = torch.empty_like(x); n = out.numel(); grid = lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(n, meta['BLOCK_SIZE']),); add_kernel[grid](x, y, out, n, BLOCK_SIZE=1024); return out. On the right, Triton thinking: one program, one whole block of a thousand elements as a vector.

It loads a full vector from x and a full vector from y in one line each.
At the end of the array, the last block hangs over the edge. A mask switches off the overhanging lanes.
It adds and stores the whole vector back. The compiler turns this into wide, coalesced loads across the warps.

hook: PyTorch's eager softmax-by-hand reads memory about four times more than it needs to. A twenty-line Triton kernel reads each row once.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — PyTorch's eager softmax-by-hand reads memory about four times more than it needs to. A twenty-line Triton kernel reads each row once.

0:15 QUESTION — The Triton fused softmax tutorial is the cleanest demonstration of why fusion matters, and it is the shape of the attention inner loop. How much faster is one kernel than five, and how close to the bandwidth limit can we get?

1:00 INTUITION — The naive version computes max, subtract, exp, sum and divide as separate PyTorch ops, each a trip to DRAM and back. The fused kernel loads a row into registers once, does all five steps there, and writes once. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — From the Triton tutorial: naive_softmax on an M x N matrix reads 5MN + 2M elements and writes 3MN + 2M. Fused: reads MN, writes MN. Expected speedup ~ (8MN + 4M) / 2MN ~ 4x. Fused kernel time lower bound: 2 x 4 x MN bytes / 1008 GB/s; at M = 4096, N = 4096 that is 134 MB, about 0.13 ms.

4:30 CODE — @triton.jit def softmax_kernel(out_ptr, in_ptr, in_row_stride, out_row_stride, n_cols, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr): row = tl.program_id(0); offs = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE); mask = offs < n_cols; x = tl.load(in_ptr + row * in_row_stride + offs, mask=mask, other=-float('inf')); x = x - tl.max(x, axis=0); num = tl.exp(x); den = tl.sum(num, axis=0); tl.store(out_ptr + row * out_row_stride + offs, num / den, mask=mask). Wrapper: BLOCK_SIZE = triton.next_power_of_2(n_cols); num_warps = 4, 8 or 16 by BLOCK_SIZE; grid = (n_rows,). Also write naive_softmax(x) in plain PyTorch ops for the comparison.

8:00 RECEIPT — torch.testing.assert_close(softmax(x), torch.softmax(x, dim=1)) for (1823, 781), the tutorial's odd shape, and for (4096, 4096). Speed: GB/s (2MN x 4 bytes) for triton, torch.softmax and naive_softmax at M = 4096 over N from 256 to 12544 using triton.testing.perf_report. Expect triton and torch.softmax near each other and well above naive, naive about 3 to 4x slower as the tutorial predicts. Compare against the 1008 GB/s roof and against my CUDA softmax from M07E10.
10:30 MEASURE — The perf_report line plot: GB/s vs N for triton, torch, naive, and my CUDA version. Mark where BLOCK_SIZE gets large enough that registers spill and throughput drops.

11:30 TAKEAWAY — Fusion turns five memory round trips into one, so memory-bound chains get close to the ideal ratio of traffic. Interview line: 'Naive softmax moves about 8MN elements, fused moves 2MN, so you expect roughly 4x, and that is what the benchmark shows.'

interview_q: Why is a fused softmax kernel faster than composing PyTorch ops? Model answer: Each eager op reads and writes the full tensor in DRAM. Each op pulls the whole matrix up to the chip, does a tiny bit of math, and pushes the result back down.
We count the arrows between memory and the chip. Eight full matrix trips in total for one softmax.
Now we switch to Triton. One program takes one row and loads the whole thing into registers.
Max, subtract, exp, sum and divide all happen right there in registers, without touching DRAM again.
One write back to memory, and the row is done. That is two trips instead of eight.
On the chart, the fused kernel sits near the bandwidth roof, about four times above the naive line.

hook: Triton's matmul tutorial gets close to cuBLAS in about fifty lines. The secret is not the math. It is the order the blocks run in.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Triton's matmul tutorial gets close to cuBLAS in about fifty lines. The secret is not the math. It is the order the blocks run in.

0:15 QUESTION — In M07E08 it took six CUDA kernels to approach cuBLAS. Triton's tl.dot handles tensor cores and shared-memory staging for you, which leaves two decisions: block sizes and launch order. How close does it get on a 4090 in fp16?

1:00 INTUITION — Each program computes one BLOCK_M by BLOCK_N tile of C by stepping through K. If programs launch in plain row order, a wave of them touches a thin strip of A but all of B, and the L2 cache thrashes. Grouping launches into small super-rows makes neighbors share both A and B tiles in L2. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Per program: acc (BM x BN, fp32) += A_tile (BM x BK) @ B_tile (BK x BN) for K/BK steps. FLOPs total 2MNK. Grouped ordering from the tutorial: num_pid_in_group = GROUP_M x num_pid_n; group_id = pid // num_pid_in_group; first_pid_m = group_id x GROUP_M; pid_m = first_pid_m + (pid % group_size_m); pid_n = (pid % num_pid_in_group) // group_size_m. The tutorial's example: for a 9 x 9 grid of blocks, computing 9 output blocks in row order loads 90 input blocks, grouped loads 54. Peak to compare: 165 TFLOPS dense fp16 and bf16 with fp32 accumulate on the 4090 per NVIDIA's Ada whitepaper.

5:30 CODE — @triton.autotune(configs=[triton.Config({'BLOCK_SIZE_M': 128, 'BLOCK_SIZE_N': 256, 'BLOCK_SIZE_K': 64, 'GROUP_SIZE_M': 8}, num_stages=3, num_warps=8), triton.Config({... 64, 256, 32, 8}, num_stages=4, num_warps=4), ... about 6 configs], key=['M', 'N', 'K']). @triton.jit def matmul_kernel(a_ptr, b_ptr, c_ptr, M, N, K, stride_am, stride_ak, stride_bk, stride_bn, stride_cm, stride_cn, BLOCK_SIZE_M: tl.constexpr, ...): grouped pid math; offs_am = (pid_m*BM + tl.arange(0, BM)) % M; a_ptrs = a_ptr + offs_am[:, None]*stride_am + offs_k[None, :]*stride_ak; acc = tl.zeros((BM, BN), dtype=tl.float32); for k in range(0, tl.cdiv(K, BK)): a = tl.load(a_ptrs, mask=offs_k[None, :] < K - k*BK, other=0.0); b = tl.load(...); acc = tl.dot(a, b, acc); advance pointers by BK*stride. c = acc.to(tl.float16); masked tl.store. Optional fused leaky_relu epilogue as in the tutorial.

12:30 TAKEAWAY — In Triton you choose tile shapes and launch order; tl.dot and autotune do the rest, and grouped ordering is what keeps L2 hit rates high. Model answer: It changes which output tiles are computed by consecutively launched programs, grouping them into blocks of GROUP_M rows. hook: Writing a forward kernel is half the job. Training needs the backward too, and deriving RMSNorm's gradient by hand is where most people get stuck.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Writing a forward kernel is half the job. Training needs the backward too, and deriving RMSNorm's gradient by hand is where most people get stuck.

0:15 QUESTION — Llama, Qwen and DeepSeek all use RMSNorm, and CS336 Assignment 2 has you write it in Triton with a hand-derived backward. Liger Kernel ships exactly this kind of fused norm. What does the gradient look like, and how do you reduce the weight gradient across rows?

1:00 INTUITION — Forward: divide each row by its root mean square, then scale by a learned gain. Backward: the gradient to x has a direct part, plus a correction because changing any x changes the row's RMS, which touches every output in the row. The gain gradient is a sum over all rows. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Row x in R^H. r = 1 / sqrt(mean(x^2) + eps). x_hat = x r. y = x_hat * g. Let u = dy * g. Then dr/dx_j = -r^3 x_j / H. dx_j = r u_j + sum_i u_i x_i (dr/dx_j) = r u_j - r^3 x_j (1/H) sum_i u_i x_i = r (u_j - x_hat_j mean(u * x_hat)). Weight gradient: dg = sum over rows of dy * x_hat. Save r per row (M floats) from the forward so the backward does not recompute it. Traffic: forward reads x, writes y; backward reads x, dy and writes dx, plus a reduction for dg.

5:30 CODE — @triton.jit def rmsnorm_fwd(x_ptr, g_ptr, y_ptr, rstd_ptr, stride, H, eps, BLOCK_H: tl.constexpr): one program per row; x = tl.load(..., mask, other=0.).to(tl.float32); ms = tl.sum(x*x, axis=0) / H; r = 1 / tl.sqrt(ms + eps); tl.store(rstd_ptr + row, r); y = x * r * g; tl.store. @triton.jit def rmsnorm_bwd(x_ptr, g_ptr, dy_ptr, rstd_ptr, dx_ptr, dg_partial_ptr, ...): load x, dy, g, r; xh = x * r; u = dy * g; dx = r * (u - xh * tl.sum(u * xh, axis=0) / H); store dx; store dy * xh into a per-row (M, H) buffer or accumulate per program into a (num_programs, H) partial buffer, then dg = partial.sum(0) in PyTorch. class TritonRMSNorm(torch.autograd.Function): forward saves x, g, rstd; backward launches rmsnorm_bwd.

9:00 RECEIPT — One: torch.autograd.gradcheck(TritonRMSNorm.apply, (x, g, eps)) with x (8, 64) and g (64,) in float64, requires_grad=True. Two: float32 and bf16 at (4096, 4096) vs torch.nn.functional.rms_norm(x, (H,), weight=g, eps=eps): assert_close on y, dx and dg (bf16 with looser tolerance). Three, CS336: the assignment's RMSNorm tests pass.

11:00 MEASURE — GB/s for forward (2 x M x H x bytes) and backward (3 x M x H x bytes plus dg) vs eager PyTorch RMSNorm, torch.compile'd RMSNorm, and the 1008 GB/s roof, at H in 1024, 4096, 8192, bf16.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — The backward is derived once on paper, saved statistics avoid recomputation, and the weight gradient is a cross-row reduction you handle with partial sums. Interview line: 'dx = r (dy*g - x_hat * mean(dy*g*x_hat)), and dg needs a reduction over rows, which I do with per-program partial sums to avoid atomics contention.' Writing backward kernels like this is the core skill for P1's FlashAttention backward.

gotchas: Doing the sum of squares in bf16 loses precision, upcast to fp32 inside the kernel; Accumulating dg with tl.atomic_add from thousands of programs is slow and nondeterministic, use partial buffers; Forgetting that masked lanes must load 0 (not garbage) or the mean of squares is wrong for H not a power of two
interview_q: Derive the backward pass of RMSNorm. Model answer: With r = (mean(x^2)+eps)^(-1/2), x_hat = x r, y = x_hat g and u = dy g, the gradient is dx = r (u - x_hat mean(u x_hat)), because every x_j affects r. The gain gradient is the sum over rows of dy times x_hat.
explainer: We see one row of activations as a bar chart, and next to it its root mean square, a single number.
Forward pass: every bar is divided by that number, then multiplied by a learned gain per column.
Now the backward pass begins. A gradient arrives from above, with one value for each output bar.
The direct path sends each gradient straight back, scaled by the gain and by one over the RMS.
But nudging any single bar also changes the RMS, which changes every output in the row.
That second path subtracts a small correction, the normalized row times the mean of gradient times normalized row.
For the gain, every row contributes gradient times normalized input, and we sum those contributions down the columns.
Finally, gradcheck compares all of this against finite differences in double precision, and our kernel passes.

hook: On an RTX 4090, moving a matmul from fp32 to bf16 can double its speed or more. The reason is separate silicon.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — On an RTX 4090, moving a matmul from fp32 to bf16 can double its speed or more. The reason is separate silicon.

0:15 QUESTION — Tensor cores are why everyone trains in bf16 and why DeepSeek-V3 and the speedrun push into FP8. They do small matrix multiplies as single instructions. What throughput do they actually deliver on our card, at each precision?

1:00 INTUITION — CUDA cores do one multiply-add per lane per clock. A tensor core does a whole small matrix multiply-accumulate, like 16 by 8 by 16, in one instruction issued by a warp. Lower precision inputs mean smaller multipliers, so more of them fit and run per clock. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Ada whitepaper peaks for the RTX 4090, dense: FP32 on CUDA cores 82.6 TFLOPS; TF32 tensor 82.6; FP16 and BF16 tensor with FP32 accumulate 165.2; FP16 with FP16 accumulate 330.3; FP8 listed at 660.6. Notice that on GeForce Ada TF32 has the same peak as plain FP32, unlike an A100 where TF32 is 156 vs 19.5 for FP32. Also note public measurements report FP8 cuBLASLt on the 4090 reaching roughly half the listed FP8 number, so we measure rather than trust. Precision: TF32 has 10 mantissa bits, BF16 7, FP8 E4M3 3. The WMMA API exposes 16 x 16 x 16 tiles; PTX mma.sync.aligned.m16n8k16 is the instruction underneath.

5:30 CODE — Benchmark at M = N = K in 1024 to 8192 using CUDA events after warmup: fp32 with torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = False; TF32 with torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = True (or torch.set_float32_matmul_precision('high')); bf16 and fp16 tensors via torch.matmul; FP8 E4M3 via torch._scaled_mm(a_fp8, b_fp8.t(), scale_a, scale_b, out_dtype=torch.bfloat16), a private API whose signature has changed between releases, so check your version. Then a tiny WMMA kernel through load_inline: nvcuda::wmma::fragment<matrix_a, 16, 16, 16, half, row_major> a_frag; load_matrix_sync, mma_sync, store_matrix_sync, one warp per 16 x 16 output tile, to show the instruction is real.

9:00 RECEIPT — Each precision's measured TFLOPs as percent of its whitepaper peak in a table. Accuracy: relative error of each against a float64 matmul on the same inputs (TF32 ~1e-3, bf16 ~1e-2, fp8 larger). WMMA kernel: assert_close vs torch.matmul(a.float(), b.float()) with fp16 tolerance.
11:00 MEASURE — Grouped bar chart: TFLOPs by precision at 8192, beside the peak. Scatter: speed vs relative error, the tradeoff in one picture.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Tensor cores deliver most of a modern GPU's FLOPs, but only for low-precision inputs and matmul-shaped work; on a 4090, bf16 is the practical sweet spot and FP8 needs scaling. Interview line: 'On H100 or A100, TF32 is a big speedup over FP32; on a GeForce 4090 it is not, because NVIDIA rates TF32 tensor throughput at the same 82.6 TFLOPS.'

interview_q: Why do tensor cores make low precision so much faster? Model answer: A tensor core computes a small matrix multiply-accumulate per instruction, and narrower inputs need smaller multipliers, so the hardware does many more multiply-adds per clock at bf16 or FP8 than at FP32. Accumulation stays in fp32 to keep sums accurate.
explainer: On the left we see a CUDA core lane doing one multiply add per clock. On the right, a tensor core.
The tensor core takes a sixteen by sixteen tile of A and a sixteen by eight tile of B in one go.
It produces a whole tile of partial results in one instruction, and adds them into an fp32 accumulator.
Now we shrink the input numbers. Thirty two bit, nineteen bit TF32, sixteen bit bf16, eight bit fp8.
Smaller numbers mean smaller multipliers, so more of them fit and the throughput bar grows at each step.
But each step also loses mantissa bits. The error bar grows right alongside the speed bar.
On the 4090, bf16 hits the sweet spot. Double the fp32 throughput, with error that training tolerates.

Fused: read x, w, b once, write once, about 2 passes plus small vectors. Predicted speedup ~ ratio of passes. hook: Time a GPU kernel with Python's time module and you will measure the launch, not the kernel. Here is a benchmark helper you can trust.
beats: 0:00 HOOK — Time a GPU kernel with Python's time module and you will measure the launch, not the kernel. Here is a benchmark helper you can trust.

0:15 QUESTION — Every number in this module came from CUDA events after warmup. GPU MODE has a whole lecture on benchmarking mistakes, and kernel leaderboards run strict harnesses for this reason. What goes wrong, and what does triton.testing.do_bench do that a naive loop does not?

1:00 INTUITION — The CPU queues kernels and moves on, so a host timer stops before the GPU finishes. Caches stay warm between repetitions, so you time an L2 hit. Clocks ramp up and throttle. The first call compiles. A good benchmark fixes each of these: sync, events, cache flush, warmup, many repeats, median. [EXPLAINER plays here]

2:30 MATH — Kernel launch overhead is a few microseconds, so any kernel shorter than about 10 microseconds is dominated by launch cost unless you batch or use CUDA graphs. Report the median and the 20th and 80th percentiles rather than the mean, because outliers from clock changes skew it. Effective throughput: GB/s = bytes / median_seconds / 1e9, TFLOPs = flops / median_seconds / 1e12. L2 flush: write a buffer larger than the 72 MB L2 before each timed call; Triton's do_bench uses a 256 MB buffer for this.

4:30 CODE — Show three wrong versions first: time.perf_counter around fn() with no sync (impossibly fast); with torch.cuda.synchronize() but no warmup (first call includes compile or cuBLAS heuristics); events but tiny inputs that live in L2. Then def bench(fn, warmup=25, rep=100, flush_l2=True, quantiles=(0.5, 0.2, 0.8)): cache = torch.empty(256 * 1024**2, dtype=torch.int8, device='cuda'); for _ in range(warmup): fn(); torch.cuda.synchronize(); starts = [torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True) for _ in range(rep)]; ends = same; for i in range(rep): if flush_l2: cache.zero_(); starts[i].record(); fn(); ends[i].record(); torch.cuda.synchronize(); times = torch.tensor([s.elapsed_time(e) for s, e in zip(starts, ends)]); return torch.quantile(times, torch.tensor(quantiles)). Plus helpers gbps(bytes, ms) and tflops(flops, ms). Mention torch.utils.benchmark.Timer as another trustworthy option, and CUDA graphs to remove launch overhead for tiny kernels.

8:30 RECEIPT — Run the same kernels through my bench(), triton.testing.do_bench(fn, warmup=25, rep=100, quantiles=[0.5, 0.2, 0.8]) and torch.utils.benchmark.Timer: vector add at 2^28, fp16 matmul at 4096, and my Triton softmax. The medians agree within about 5 percent. The naive perf_counter version is off by orders of magnitude for small kernels; show the number.

10:30 MEASURE — Plot: measured time vs input size with and without L2 flush, showing the cliff at 72 MB. Plot: time per call for a tiny kernel, eager launches vs replayed through torch.cuda.CUDAGraph, showing the launch-overhead floor. Run nvidia-smi --query-gpu=clocks.sm,temperature.gpu,power.draw during a long matmul to show clock drift.

12:00 TAKEAWAY — Warm up, synchronize, time with CUDA events, flush L2, take the median of many runs, and state the hardware peak next to every number. Interview line: 'GPU work is asynchronous, so I time with CUDA events after warmup, flush L2 between reps, and report median plus percentiles against the theoretical roof.' This bench() is reused for every kernel in M08 and P1.

interview_q: How do you correctly benchmark a CUDA kernel from PyTorch? Model answer: Warm up to exclude compilation and autotuning, record torch.cuda.Event pairs around each call, synchronize before reading elapsed_time, flush L2 between reps if you want DRAM-level numbers, and report the median of many runs alongside bytes or FLOPs as a fraction of peak.
explainer: We see two timelines, the CPU on top and the GPU below. A Python timer starts and stops on the CPU line.
The CPU launches the kernel and races ahead. The timer stops long before the GPU block even finishes.
So we place CUDA events on the GPU line itself, one before the kernel and one after.
The first run includes compilation and shows up as a giant block. So we throw away the warmup runs.
Between repetitions the data sits in L2. We sweep a big buffer through the cache to push it out.
A hundred timed runs form a histogram. We report the median and the spread, not the mean.
Our helper, Triton's do bench and PyTorch's Timer now report the same number within a few percent.

linkedin: Closed the kernels module by building the benchmarking helper I will reuse for the rest of the series: warmup, per-repetition CUDA events, L2 flushing, and median with percentiles. It agrees with triton.testing.do_bench and torch.utils.benchmark within about 5 percent, while a naive host timer was off by orders of magnitude on small kernels. Every number I publish from here on goes through it.
